Demand
Macro backdrop

blocks.html: The macro frame improved at the margin. Barclays’ economists revised 3Q26 growth up materially: global GDP is now put at 3.5% saar (up 0.8ppt on the 18 September 2026 edition) and the US at 3.4% (up 0.9ppt), while France was cut to a 0.5% contraction. The upgrade is backward-looking. From 4Q26 the forecasts are broadly unchanged, with the US at 2.0% and the euro area at or below 1.1% through 2Q27. GS points the same way, expecting US real GDP to grow by an average of ~2.2% over the next four quarters and Europe by ~1.1%. For a lessor book this is slow but positive growth: it supports traffic outside the conflict region without giving airlines a demand-led way out of high fuel costs.

blocks.text: Global passenger traffic

blocks.html: Traffic is weak but no longer deteriorating. IATA reported global RPKs down 0.5% yoy in September 2026, after a 0.8% decline in August, with the industry load factor at 83.2% (down 0.3ppt yoy); excluding the Middle East, demand grew 0.3%. International traffic returned to growth (up 0.4%, or 1.7% excluding Middle East carriers) while domestic traffic fell 2.2%, with India (down 8.3%) and the US (down 2.7%) the weak spots. IATA’s full-year 2026 traffic growth forecast of 2.1% dates from its June outlook and has not been updated; monthly prints from May to September ran between a 2.2% decline and a 0.2% gain, so the forecast now looks demanding. The September release gives no year-to-date figure (n.d.).

blocks.html: By region (Exhibit 2) the drag sits in two places: the Middle East, down 8.0%, and North America, down 1.6%. Africa (up 5.0%) and Latin America (up 4.3%) lead, while Asia-Pacific (up 0.5%) and Europe (up 0.3%) are marginally positive. Against May, the Middle East decline has narrowed sharply (from 28.4%) and North America has weakened (from a 0.8% decline). The Fund’s exposure is 54.4% APAC and 31.2% Americas (Exhibit 10), so its largest region is growing slowly and its second-largest is contracting on US domestic weakness.

blocks.html: Capacity remains disciplined. GS shows global forward scheduled capacity growing 1/2/3% yoy in October, November and December, against 2/3/3% for August to October in its prior edition; October itself was cut from 3% to 1%. IATA’s chief economist expects scheduled capacity to stay above 2025 levels in October and November but calls growth weak and uneven. Airlines are protecting load factors and yields at the expense of volume, which is the outcome a lessor prefers.

blocks.text: US demand

blocks.html: The US is where volume and price have diverged most. North American RPKs fell 1.6% yoy in September and US domestic traffic fell 2.7% (IATA), yet GS reports average US airline yields up 12.0% yoy in 2Q26, from 6.7% in 1Q26, and Barclays’ screen-scraped North Atlantic economy fares were up 36% at American and 34% at United in September. Barclays expects RASK to lag fares as loads fade. US business jet operations slowed to 3% growth in September from 7% in July. US airlines are raising price to cover fuel while flying less; that protects near-term lessee credit but is not a sign of demand strength. Barclays’ October edition does not repeat the TSA volume reference used in last quarter’s dashboard.

blocks.text: European airline pricing & consumer demand

blocks.html: European pricing turned in September. Barclays’ data shows intra-Europe short-haul fares up yoy at all three flag-carrier groups - Lufthansa Group 10%, AF-KLM 2% and IAG 2% - against declines of 2%, 6% and 8% in August. North Atlantic economy fares strengthened further (IAG up 36%, Lufthansa Group 32%, AF-KLM 18%). Among low-cost carriers Ryanair’s decline narrowed to 1% from 10%, Vueling rose 10% and Wizz Air stayed weakest, down 13%. Barclays treats the direction as credible and the scale with caution, and notes that bookings have shifted close-in.

blocks.html: UK card spending on airlines turned positive, up 1% yoy over the 28 days to 23 October 2026 (-1.6% in the prior edition), driven by the over-64 cohort (up 10.1%) while 18-29s were still down 7.2%. Vueling, an IAG subsidiary, is a lessee in the Fund’s first portfolio pool, and TAP Portugal and Air France are in the second, so firmer European fares are a modest positive for those credits.

blocks.text: Airline profitability & fuel

blocks.html: Profitability guidance is unchanged and ageing. IATA’s June outlook still puts 2026 industry net profit at US$23bn on a 2.0% net margin, down from US$45bn and 4.2% in 2025, with a record 84.0% load factor and jet fuel averaging US$152/bbl (US$90/bbl in 2025). IATA normally updates the outlook in December.

blocks.html: Fuel has moved in the lessees’ favour since the last issue. US Gulf Coast jet fuel spot was US$3.76/gal on 17 November 2026, down 14.5% from US$4.40/gal on 29 September 2026 and from a peak of US$4.69/gal on 23 October 2026 (EIA data). That is about 4% above the US$3.62/gal implied by IATA’s assumption (Junson calculation at 42 gallons per barrel), against roughly 22% above at the end of September. If spot holds near the assumption, the downside risk to IATA’s US$23bn narrows; the December outlook will show whether weaker traffic offsets it. Both readings use the Gulf Coast series, so they are comparable with each other but not with the New York Harbor quote used in the last issue.

blocks.text: Supply
Order backlog & deliveries

blocks.html: Order flow remains strong and lumpy. GS reports Boeing booked 165 gross orders with 0 cancellations and Airbus 17 with 3 in September, against 38 and 204 gross orders in July. Trade press attributes Boeing’s 165 to October and largely to a single lessor - Avolon’s firm order for 140 737 MAX 10s after the type’s FAA certification on 20 October 2026; we keep the GS month label and flag the discrepancy. The backlog reference is unchanged at more than 18,000 aircraft (IATA, May 2026, as cited by the GP).

blocks.html: Deliveries are the constraint. Boeing delivered 31 737 MAX in October against 43 in September, is holding at a rate of 42 a month and has said it will miss its goal of 500 MAX deliveries this year; Airbus delivered 74 aircraft in October. Slower narrowbody output extends the period in which airlines rely on leased in-service aircraft. That supports the Fund’s 737 and A320-family positions, and makes the remaining VietJet 737-8 deliveries the item to confirm.

blocks.text: Supply normalisation watch

blocks.html: The evidence this quarter is mixed, and thinner than last quarter because the JPM lessor report that carried the normalisation argument was not provided. Pointing to loosening: parked aircraft rose to 11.4% of the fleet in September from 11.1% in July (Cirium, via GS), the MAX 10 is certified, and a 140-aircraft lessor order shows lessors positioning for higher output. Pointing to continued tightness: Boeing’s production shortfall and sale-leasebacks at about 31% of 2025 deliveries (Cirium, via GS). We have no appraiser data this quarter to test whether the decline in mid-life narrowbody values and lease rates continued.

Lessor portfolio economics

blocks.html: The one public read is AerCap’s third-quarter result of 28 October 2026. AerCap sold 70 owned assets for US$1.1bn at a 45% unlevered gain-on-sale margin, booking US$353m of gains, while basic lease rents were flat yoy at US$1,698m (US$1,690m a year earlier). Net spread was 8.1% and the average cost of debt 4.2%. Management said higher fuel prices are hurting airline profitability but supply-demand fundamentals still favour lessors. Secondary-market pricing therefore remains well above book for the largest seller, consistent with the multiples the GP reports on the Fund’s own monetisations; flat rents on a shrinking owned fleet say less about market lease rates.

Airline credit backdrop

blocks.html: GS shows high-yield airline debt trading roughly in line with the broad high-yield market, as last quarter. For the Fund’s lessees the quarter’s events were positive: Portugal selected Lufthansa to buy an initial 44.9% of TAP for €1.025bn on 14 October 2026, and jet fuel fell. Against that, the Middle East traffic decline (8.0%) bears on Flynas (7.5% of exposure) and weak US domestic traffic on the Fund’s US lessees.

blocks.html: GP narrative (Bain Capital Griffin, Q2 2026 letter; no newer letter): the GP describes “a cost crisis for airline owners rather than a demand crisis for aircraft”. This quarter’s sell-side data is consistent with the first half of that sentence and tests the second: fares and yields are up and fuel is off its high, but global traffic fell yoy in four of the five months from May to September. The gap between the GP’s view and the market data has neither opened nor closed, and it cannot be judged properly until the GP’s third-quarter letter and a lessor-credit report are in hand.

items: Quarter activity (as reported for 2Q26, not new): the Fund funded the aircraft portfolio acquired in the first quarter, taking capital called to 36.0% of commitments (ITD contributions US$127.1M); those aircraft went into the platform’s second Master Trust ABS issuance of US$568M in June. One monetisation had closed and five were in progress; ITD distributions were US$6.2M, with a further US$12.7M distributed after quarter-end.

Manager commentary (Q2 letter): the GP sees a cost crisis for airline owners rather than a demand crisis for aircraft, says the Fund is tracking above its high-single-digit distributable cash yield target, and expected a meaningfully sized final close in October. We have no confirmation of that close.

blocks.html: The Fund has sourced five transactions; pro forma for monetisations executed and in progress it holds 29x aircraft and 5x engines. The portfolio stands at US$1,352M on a purchase-price basis against the US$3,750M scaled target (36%, from ~33% at 1Q26), with about US$1.1bn of delivered and committed assets. Two transactions make up most of the value: Portfolio Acquisition #2 at 40% and VietJet at 32%, followed by United at 19%.

blocks.html: The GP’s exposure chart as of 30 June 2026 (Exhibit 10, redrawn with monetised assets in grey) shows a narrowbody book: 81.4% narrowbody, with 737 MAX at 44.0% and A320ceo at 21.7%, and 14.9% of exposure monetised or in the process. By lessee, VietJet (27.6%) and United (16.4%) dominate, followed by Lion Air (9.5%) and Flynas (7.5%). By region the book is 54.4% APAC, 31.2% Americas and 2.7% Europe. Tier 1 and Tier 2 credits are 45.6% of exposure excluding monetised assets (59.0% including them) against a scaled target of ~75%, which is why the GP scores lessee counterparty as near rather than meeting target; Tier 3 is 39.5%. Read against this quarter’s market data, the VietJet and Lion Air weight sits in the slow-growing Asia-Pacific region and the United weight in the contracting US market, while the Middle East exposure is limited to Flynas.

blocks.text: Fund level performance detail

blocks.html: Fund-level ITD IRR, MoM and DPI remain not meaningful with the Fund under 50% called. At the investment level, gross performance on US$194.4M invested (all unrealised at 30 June 2026) stood at >50% gross IRR and 1.60x gross MoM; NAV was US$227.6M (64.5% of the US$353.0M commitments) and ITD proceeds realised US$39.4M. We lean on MoM over IRR for holds this short. Closed monetisations returned 1.40x (United, JOLCO) and 2.11x (ex-Spirit); the pending ones carry GP estimates of 1.82x to 2.95x, which are estimates until closing is reported.
